title: Empathy ability in patients with schizophrenia-spectrum disorders: Subjective assessment and experimental study data
abstract: Context and relevance. Empathy is a multifactorial ability that determines the quality of interpersonal relationships and the level of social adaptation. Research on empathy in patients with schizophrenia spectrum disorders (SSD) yields mixed results: some studies show significant deficits, while others do not confirm these differences. A possible explanation for these contradictions is the limitations of self-report methods in measuring empathic abilities, with a noted lack of both domestic and international studies in which self-report data are compared with results from experimental measures of empathy. The relevance of such studies is determined by the need to identify the most accurate methods for assessing empathy in individuals with SSD and to highlight empathy deficits that are specific to this group. Objective: to compare subjective assessments of empathic ability with data obtained from experimental research. Hypothesis. Indicators of empathic abilities in patients with schizophrenia and schizoaffective disorder, measured using questionnaire-based methods, are higher than those obtained through experimental approaches, as patients with RSD often underestimate their level of empathic deficit. Methods and materials. The study involved 53 participants: 36 patients with schizophrenia spectrum disorders and 17 mentally healthy controls, aged 21 to 50 years (mean age: M = 30.1, SD = 8.8 for patients; M = 30, SD = 7 for controls). The sample included 30 males and 23 females. To achieve the research aim, the following instruments were used: the Symptomatic Questionnaire SCL-90, the Hospital Anxiety and Depression Scale (HADS) for assessing psychopathological symptoms, the Davis Interpersonal Reactivity Index (IRI), and the modification of Fyodor Vasilyuk and Elena Sheryagina’s Technique of “Comforting Strategies” for evaluating empathic ability. Results. No significant differences were found between the groups in empathy indicators measured via the IRI questionnaire: patients with schizophrenia spectrum disorders assessed their capacities for perspective-taking, compassion, and empathic concern at levels comparable to healthy controls (p > 0.05). The only significant difference was in empathic distress: during interpersonal situations involving others' feelings in crises, patients with RSD experienced more intense anxiety than controls. In the “Comforting Strategies” task, patients with schizoaffective disorder more frequently employed responses related to formal or counter-support (i.e., responses not aimed at normalizing the emotional state of the other person and even exacerbating their discomfort). Their ability to provide reflexive and emotional support was lower than that of the control group (p < 0.01). Conclusions. Empathy indicators obtained via questionnaire methods in patients with schizophrenia and schizoaffective disorder are higher than those derived from experimental assessments. Patients with schizophrenia spectrum disorders more often than healthy individuals provide unproductive support, indicating that they tend to underestimate their level of empathic deficit. Questionnaire-based methods are insufficiently effective for assessing empathic ability in these patients, as they fail to reveal existing deficits in empathic responsiveness to the emotional states of others.
